documents.title: HFSA Expert consensus on heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

chunks.content: Nonstandard Abbreviation and Acronym GDMT goal‐directed medical therapy Clinical Perspective What Is New? We report a standardized approach to assessing for ventricular recovery in pediatric patients with ventricular assist device support. This approach centers on a core set of components, including a cultural shift, universal use of reverse remodeling medications, a stepwise evaluation of ventricular function recovery by echocardiography, exercise testing, and catheterization, as well as a multidisciplinary discussion to present findings. What Are the Clinical Implications? There may be higher rates of ventricular recovery in pediatric patients with cardiomyopathy supported with a ventricular assist device than previously identified. The use of ventricular assist devices (VAD) in the pediatric population continues to increase, with 1430 devices placed in 1220 patients between April 2018 and June 2023, , and VAD therapy has become the standard of care for children with refractory advanced heart failure. Although VAD therapy has traditionally been used as a bridge to transplant in pediatric patients, mechanical unloading of the failing heart also promotes ventricular recovery and has contributed to a small number of reported successful explants, with rates ranging from 2% to 33%. , , , , Given that pediatric heart transplantation comes with both short‐term and long‐term morbidity and mortality, and even patients who do well will be faced with decisions about retransplant in early adulthood, the potential for ventricular recovery and explant has critical clinical implications for children. Recent work in adult patients supported on durable LVAD has suggested that the incidence of ventricular recovery is underappreciated, and given the plasticity inherent to pediatric myocardium, we suspect that a similar phenomenon may be occurring in children. Based on these premises, we developed and implemented a programmatic effort to promote and identify ventricular recovery in patients with durable VADs cared for at our center. We report our approach and the early results in the following article. Methods This retrospective cohort study was performed at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, a quaternary pediatric care center that implants between 15 and 20 durable VADs annually. Patients who underwent VAD implant between October 2022 and October 2024 were reviewed and outcomes measured through April 2025 to allow for a minimum of 3 months of clinical follow‐up for all patients. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board, and given the retrospective nature of data collection, informed consent was waived. Deidentified study data and statistical methods will be shared on request after execution of a data use agreement. An intentional programmatic change initiated in October 2022 included 4 core components (Figure ): (1) cultural shift: recovery of ventricular function is assessed in all patients on VAD, for consideration of potential explant, or in the case of complex congenital heart disease (CHD), for further surgical palliation; (2) reverse remodeling—all VAD patients are placed on goal‐directed medical therapy (GDMT) as tolerated; (3) implementation of a stepwise protocolized assessment of recovery using echocardiography, exercise testing, and cardiac catheterization; and (4) multidisciplinary meetings to discuss and optimize patients identified as responders. Responders were defined as patients who demonstrated an improvement in LV ejection fraction ≥45%, atrioventricular valve regurgitation by ≥1 grade, and normalization of LV end diastolic dimension Z score to ≤2.5. Culture Shift Traditionally, our institutional practice has been to consider VAD therapy as a bridge to transplant for almost all patients and reserve consideration of ventricular recovery for a select few thought to have the most favorable preimplant characteristics. However, in October 2022, we intentionally changed our approach for children on durable VAD. Rather than assuming heart transplant as the end point, for patients with biventricular physiology, we chose to evaluate for ventricular recovery to support VAD explantation. For those with CHD or single ventricle physiology, we applied a similar evaluative pathway to assess for the potential to reconsider surgical strategies. The implementation of a weekly VAD‐focused bedside rounds allowed for a targeted time to assess ventricular function and recovery in each patient, review medical therapy, and evaluate optimal pump settings. These rounds also include interdisciplinary conversations on assessment of recovery to facilitate a shared mental model and consistent approach to patient care. The cultural shift toward prioritizing recovery as a primary goal of care at our institution can be contextualized using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, particularly within the “inner setting” domain. Key components included leadership engagement across heart failure, critical care, and surgical teams; structured multidisciplinary education to increase awareness and knowledge of recovery potential; and repeated reinforcement of recovery goals during daily rounds and team meetings. These strategies help establish an “implementation climate” in which recovery is viewed as both feasible and desirable. Importantly, consistent messaging from clinical champions and embedding messages in the routine workflow supported these efforts, characteristics that Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research identifies as critical to successful implementation. These strategies help establish an “implementation climate” in which recovery is viewed as both feasible and desirable. Importantly, consistent messaging from clinical champions and embedding messages in the routine workflow supported these efforts, characteristics that Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research identifies as critical to successful implementation. Framing our cultural shift in this way underscores the importance of deliberate, system‐level strategies in changing ingrained clinical assumptions and may serve as a model for other institutions aiming to adopt similar protocols. This change in orientation led to a series of more specific practice changes discussed later. Goal‐Directed Medical Therapy To promote ventricular recovery, all patients on durable VAD are started on GDMT, which is gradually increased to goal dosing in accordance with the recently published ACTION (Advanced Cardiac Therapies Improving Outcomes Network) guidelines. In general, medications are incorporated in a stepwise fashion once the patient has demonstrated hemodynamic stability and include either an angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitor, angiotensin receptor blocker, or angiotensin receptor/neprilysin inhibitor; beta blocker; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; and digoxin, in alignment with the RESTAGE‐HF (Remission from Stage D Heart Failure) protocol. Over time, this regimen has evolved to include a SGLT2 (sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2) inhibitor for certain patients. For those patients who do not tolerate medication introduction during an initial attempt, due to either hypotension or kidney dysfunction, repeat attempts are made, guided by the belief that tolerance of GDMT offers the best opportunity for recovery. Stepwise Assessment of Ventricular Recovery Based on our hypothesis that a standardized and regular assessment of ventricular recovery would promote its recognition, we developed the following protocolized assessments for patients on VAD support, as demonstrated in Figure . Echocardiogram During the period immediately following VAD implant, settings are optimized to promote myocardial rest and end‐organ rehabilitation. All patients on VAD support have at least monthly surveillance echocardiograms regardless of initial diagnosis or clinical course. For those patients meeting echocardiographic criteria (LV end diastolic dimension Z score ≤2.5, ejection fraction ≥45%, and ≤mild mitral regurgitation), and who have been on support for ≥2 months, an echocardiographic turndown study at the bedside is performed. During the study, VAD support is gradually decreased, and echocardiography is used to assess LV size and function, mitral regurgitation, and evidence of increased right ventricular pressure estimates as a surrogate for left atrial hypertension. For patients supported with the Berlin Heart EXCOR, baseline coagulation laboratory values, as well as complete blood count, complete metabolic profile, and BNP (brain natriuretic peptide), are obtained before all echocardiographic turndown studies, and the pump is assessed for fibrin/clot deposition. Turndown studies are deferred if the patient has an active infection or there are concerns about inadequate anticoagulation. Patients undergoing an echocardiographic turndown study are anticoagulated with bolus doses of heparin, in addition to their current bivalirudin infusion, and the VAD rate does not decrease below 50 bpm until the activated clotting time is confirmed to be >250 on point‐of‐care testing. Assessment of vital signs, clinical status, and echocardiogram takes place, whereas the VAD is decreased at a cadence of 20 beats every 3 to 5 minutes. If the patient is tolerating the trial, a decision may be made to move to hand pumping, mimicking an off‐pump trial, for 15 to 30 minutes. Final images, vital signs, and laboratory values are obtained subsequently. Laboratory values at the nadir of turndown include blood gas with lactate, complete metabolic profile, and BNP. For patients on HeartMate3 (HM3) support, the process is similar. After obtaining baseline laboratory studies and confirming adequate anticoagulation, the pump speed is decreased by 200 rpm at intervals of 3 to 5 minutes. For an echocardiographic turndown, the speed is not decreased <4000 rpm and the nadir may be higher than that if there is echocardiographic evidence of reversal of flow through the outflow graft or the calculated pump flow is ≤1 L/min. Regardless of the device type, an echocardiographic turndown is considered successful if the ejection fraction remains >45% throughout the study, mitral regurgitation is no more than mild, there is no evidence of significant increase in RV pressure, and the LV does not become substantially dilated ( Z score ≥2.5). Turndown parameters were chosen based on prior literature, ACTION Harmonized Guidelines, and the Berlin EXCOR Weaning and Explantation recommendations. If a patient’s echocardiographic turndown trial is not successful, an additional attempt will be made within 3 months if the patient remains on the device. Turndown parameters were chosen based on prior literature, ACTION Harmonized Guidelines, and the Berlin EXCOR Weaning and Explantation recommendations. If a patient’s echocardiographic turndown trial is not successful, an additional attempt will be made within 3 months if the patient remains on the device. Exercise Stress Testing If a patient has a successful echocardiographic turndown and can participate in exercise stress testing (EST), we advance to an EST with VAD turndown. This testing has been shown to be helpful in adult patients being considered for explant. , Again, baseline laboratory values and echocardiographic images are obtained, and the VAD speed is decreased to a lower speed determined during the prior echocardiographic turndown. The patient then performs an EST on these low VAD settings, with repeat echocardiogram performed at peak exertion. VAD parameters, vital signs, and ECG are monitored throughout the EST. Successful exercise parameters include maximum VO 2 >20 mL/kg/min, the absence of exercise‐associated ectopy and symptoms, and echocardiographic findings of improved ventricular function at peak exertion. The change in pulsatility index during EST is also monitored; noting a high pulsatility index (≥10) may indicate increased contractility and correspond to improved ventricular function. Cardiac Catheterizations Patients who have demonstrated successful bedside echocardiographic turndowns and successful EST (when applicable) are referred for cardiac catheterization. Whenever possible, patients are maintained on their baseline regimens of anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy throughout the catheterization. During the procedure, additional heparin is administered to maintain an activated clotting time ≥250 s for the duration of the case to minimize the risk of periprocedural ischemic stroke. During the catheterization, echocardiographic images, hemodynamic measurements, and laboratory studies are obtained during 3 different conditions. For patients supported on the Berlin Heart EXCOR, data are gathered at the patient’s baseline rate, at 35 bpm, and after 15 minutes of hand pumping at a rate of 6 bpm. For those supported with an HM3 device, data are obtained at the patient’s baseline rpm, 4000 rpm, and the nadir. The goal is to decrease the speed on the HM3 to the point where the calculated flow is ~1 L/min, which is thought be enough flow to prevent reversal of blood through the outflow graft but not a substantial amount of VAD cardiac output. Successful hemodynamic parameters include pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (<13 mm Hg), normal cardiac index, and a normal mixed venous saturation (>70%). Multidisciplinary Meetings For patients who have completed the preceding steps, a multidisciplinary team meeting is held to further discuss potential VAD explant. Over time, and by comparing the courses of patients evaluated for recovery, we have developed an explant readiness checklist to help guide our discussion (Figure ). An example of a patient’s progression through turndown trials and evaluation in the explant readiness evaluation is depicted in Figure . These meetings include members from our heart failure/transplant team, surgical representatives, advance cardiac therapies intensive care unit and stepdown unit members, rehabilitation team, psychosocial team, and nursing. This diverse group of members allows for a robust and holistic assessment of patient progress. Given the relatively high incidence of early failure after explant, a discussion with the intensive care unit and surgical teams about potential future mechanical support options is a critical component of this discussion. Finally, if the medical team agrees that explant has a reasonable chance of success, a discussion is held with the family to determine the appropriate next steps. To augment these individual patient discussions, and iteratively improve our process, we perform biannual reviews of patients undergoing explant evaluation or who were previously explanted. Our surgical approach to explant differs by device. For HM3, we preferentially used a titanium plug. Although there can be logistical hurdles to obtaining the plug, it comes with the potential advantage of a more straightforward reimplantation of the VAD if needed. We excise as much of the outflow graft as possible to limit infectious risk. For the EXCOR, the surgical strategy differs based on the anatomy. In certain cases, we use primary closure at the cannulation site, and in others, a small patch is used. Statistical Analysis The primary outcome of interest was whether a patient underwent VAD explant for myocardial recovery. Permutation 1‐way tests were used to compare continuous variables and Fisher exact tests were used to compare categorical variables. Data are described as medians with interquartile range for continuous variables and counts with percentages for categorical variables. Significance was established a priori at an α level of 0.05. All statistical analysis was performed using R Statistical Software (version 4.5.1). Results Demographic and Clinical Characteristics From October 2022 to October 2024, there were 35 patients

Results Demographic and Clinical Characteristics From October 2022 to October 2024, there were 35 patients supported with durable VADs, including 22 (63%) with a paracorporeal device and 13 (37%) with an HM3. Most patients had a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy (60%, N=21), followed in incidence by CHD (31%, N=11), ischemic cardiomyopathy (6%, N=2), and myocarditis (3%, N=1). We felt that ischemic cardiomyopathy in the setting of anomalous left coronary arising from the pulmonary artery, or a neonatal coronary thrombus represented different underlying pathophysiology of ventricular dysfunction than other CHD and therefore grouped them separately. There were significant differences in underlying diagnosis; there were no patients with CHD who were explanted for recovery; however, 38% of patients without CHD in this cohort were explanted ( P =0.006). There was also a significant difference in GDMT tolerance between the cohorts with all patients who got explanted tolerating ≥3 medications ( P <0.001). There were no statistically significant differences in age, sex, INTERMACS (Interagency Registry of Mechanically Assisted Circulatory Support) at time of implant, device type, or duration of support that were identified (Tables and ). Patients who underwent explant had between 1 and 3 cardiac catheterizations performed (median 2 catheterizations). Postcatheterization complications were rare, with no serious adverse events, and 1 patient who experienced access site bleeding that resolved after direct manual pressure was applied. Explanted Patients: Characteristics Characteristics of the 9 patients explanted for recovery are shown in Tables and Table . Patient age at the time of implant ranged from 3 months to 15 years old. Two explanted patients were supported with HM3 devices; the remaining 7 patients were supported primarily with Berlin Heart EXCOR. One of the patients was briefly supported on CentriMag in the immediate postoperative period before transitioning to Berlin Heart EXCOR for longer term management. Eight of the 9 patients explanted had their VAD placed during their index heart failure admission. Due to severity of illness, only 3 of the 9 patients received a cardiac magnetic resonance imaging before VAD. One patient demonstrated positive criteria for myocarditis by edema and markedly elevated extracellular volume. The remaining 2 patients demonstrated chronic ventricular dilation and dysfunction; 1 demonstrated top normal diffuse fibrosis and a coronary artery anomaly thought to be an incidental finding. All patients who reached explant had normal or mildly diminished systolic function by echocardiogram, and none had a wedge pressure during catheterization turndown of >14 mm Hg. Notably, 2 infants in this cohort had a pronounced left bundle‐branch block on presenting ECG and profound dyssynchrony on echocardiogram that was thought to potentiate their ventricular dysfunction. Both patients underwent placement of cardiac resynchronization therapy pacemaker system at the time of explant. Explanted Patients Outcomes Of the 9 patients who reached explant, all were discharged from the hospital with median follow‐up time of 10 months (interquartile range, 5.5–20 months). On most recent clinical evaluations, all explanted patients had mildly diminished or normalized systolic function. Four of 9 patients have had readmissions since explant. One patient, a teenager with a history of tachycardia‐associated cardiomyopathy, was readmitted shortly after discharge with palpitations. There was no ectopy observed during a 24‐hour observation or on follow‐up ambulatory rhythm monitoring, and he remains free of heart failure or tachycardia reoccurrence 11 months after his explant. The 3 other readmissions were in infants and related to concerns about nutrition and weight gain. One was admitted in the setting of social instability and discharged after 48 hours with increased outpatient support. The second patient has a comorbid neurodevelopmental condition thought to explain their feeding difficulties and was discharged after gastrostomy tube placement and is now demonstrating normal weight gain. The final patient was readmitted several times with failure to thrive that resolved temporarily. However, serial surveillance showed increasing left atrial and ventricular size and worsening pulmonary hypertension. She has subsequently been placed on milrinone and has been relisted for heart transplant. Discussion Given the increasing number of children being supported with durable VADs, the finite nature of suitable donors, and the profound implications of avoiding or deferring heart transplant in childhood, developing systems that promote and identify ventricular recovery should be a major goal in the care of pediatric patients on VAD support. Discussion Given the increasing number of children being supported with durable VADs, the finite nature of suitable donors, and the profound implications of avoiding or deferring heart transplant in childhood, developing systems that promote and identify ventricular recovery should be a major goal in the care of pediatric patients on VAD support. Over 2 years, we implemented a ventricular recovery initiative at our center, and our experience yields several important findings, lessons learned, and opportunities for further work. First, our experience demonstrates the feasibility of implementing a ventricular recovery program in a pediatric heart center. We believe that a protocolized approach to assessment of ventricular function, discussion of data at a regularly scheduled multidisciplinary meeting, and maximally tolerated GDMT are key factors in the successful implementation of such a program. Data in adults on durable left VAD show promising outcomes for those patients on GDMT, , and successful protocolized recovery programs have prioritized this. Considering this, we have made an emphasis on placing our patients on these agents. Notably, 100% of the patients who underwent explant were receiving ≥3 GDMT agents. Whether this relationship is causative or not merits additional study. In the 28 months before the interventions described, we placed durable VADs in 29 patients, only 1 of whom was explanted for myocardial recovery. This difference emphasizes the potential benefits of creating a dedicated program to promote and identify myocardial recovery in pediatric patients on durable VAD support. Recognition of clinical progress as well as ventricular recovery through regular testing resulted in a relatively high incidence of VAD explant; in fact, over the observed period, of the 17 patients without CHD supported with durable VADs, more underwent VAD explant than heart transplant. Notably, the majority of patients who underwent explant had VAD implanted during their first admission for heart failure, suggesting that chronicity of heart failure may have an important relationship with the potential for ventricular recovery. Eight of the 9 patients who were explanted went into VAD as an INTERMACS 2 (Table ), including inability to wean from inotropes, extubate, or tolerate feeds. The indication for VAD at our institution is aligned with national practice, and therefore, we expect that patients on durable VAD support included in this study are comparable to patients on VAD across the country. However, this may highlight the need to expand the protocol to a larger and more heterogeneous cohort in order to measure the potential for reproducibility. Additionally, the fact that nearly 40% of patients without CHD underwent explant for recovery suggests that for children with heart failure unassociated with underlying CHD, the use of a VAD as a bridge to potential myocardial recovery may be especially relevant. Although the difference in age between the explanted and nonexplanted cohort did not reach statistical significance, it is notable that among the 9 patients who underwent explanation, 6 were infants aged 4 weeks to 14 months (67% of the recovered cohort). The predominance of infants among recovered patients may reflect the plasticity of the infant myocardium or their shorter duration of heart failure; however, further studies focused on understanding the mechanisms of recovery are clearly needed. Although none of the patients with CHD on VAD support in this initial cohort met the threshold to explant and reconsider surgical strategies, we have continued the process of optimizing GDMT. Over 60% of the total cohort who did not exhibit recovery were maintained on at least 2 GDMT agents. Our institution continues to evaluate for recovery in the hopes that eligible patients will be identified in a larger sample size and as our ability to discriminate improves. Several other programs have described their experiences with evaluation for ventricular recovery and VAD explant among pediatric patients and have presented encouraging findings. Langanecha et al. describe a similar process to ours with slightly more permissive hemodynamic parameters on testing (eg, wedge pressure <15 mm Hg rather than 13 mm Hg and an LV end diastolic dimension Z score <3 rather than 2.5) and have reported a recovery incidence of 12%. Miera et al. also describe their approach to myocardial recovery over 26 years, during which time they were able to explant 14.2% of patients on durable support, including several with underlying CHD. Although there exist core similarities among these approaches, their heterogeneity naturally suggests that a protocolized multicenter approach to ventricular recovery in pediatric patients on durable VAD support is needed. All patients who underwent explant have had encouraging short‐term outcomes with no incidence of death or VAD reimplantation during the follow‐up period. Although there exist core similarities among these approaches, their heterogeneity naturally suggests that a protocolized multicenter approach to ventricular recovery in pediatric patients on durable VAD support is needed. All patients who underwent explant have had encouraging short‐term outcomes with no incidence of death or VAD reimplantation during the follow‐up period. All the early postexplant periods were uneventful, which is significant given the reported high incidence of failure within 30 days of explant. In part, we attribute this success in the postoperative period to extensive collaboration with the intensive care unit team. Unless there is a clinical contraindication, patients receive left atrial monitoring lines, and for those large enough, a Swan‐Ganz catheter is placed for postoperative monitoring. Of the 8 patients who continue to be followed at our center, half have had no readmissions since their initial discharge, and of the remaining 4 patients, 3 had clinical concerns that were addressed without escalation of cardiac support. In contrast to Itagaki et al., who reported 40% continued listing or relisting for transplant after explant, our cohort had only 1 patient out of 9 who required reactivation of transplant listing, and none have required mechanical circulatory support. For certain pediatric patients supported with VAD, cardiac recovery and device explant may offer better outcomes than proceeding toward heart transplant. However, a bridge to recovery strategy comes with the risk of an event while on device and potentially of an unsuccessful explant. Thus, understanding characteristics that are favorable prognostic factors for cardiac recovery can help in the selection of patients suitable for a bridge to recovery approach, thereby improving our approach to caring for children with refractory advanced heart failure. Historically, our center targeted reversible causes as those to evaluate for explant; however, this change in practice identified 6 patients with an underlying cardiomyopathy who showed signs of recovery. Many patients had multiple catheterizations/turn down trials, emphasizing the need to continue to evaluate candidacy throughout the VAD course. Given our inability to accurately predict who will be an explant candidate, and the inherent risk of being on VAD support, it is important to mention our approach to listing these patients for heart transplant. This practice varies by VAD type as the risk of paracorporeal and intracorporeal VAD differs. For patients on HM3, we typically defer transplant listing for 3 months after implant for all patients to allow time for rehabilitation and end organ recovery. A discussion with the family is then had to discuss the perceived likelihood of recovery and explant, and a decision made to either list for transplant or remain on long‐term device therapy. For patients with Berlin Heart EXCOR, our approach differs somewhat based on the cause of heart failure. In those patients with disease processes thought more likely to be reversible, such as myocarditis, we often delay listing for heart transplant until we have a better sense of the clinical trajectory. For patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, we generally use a parallel strategy, with transplant listing simultaneous with evaluation of ventricular function recovery. In those patients who demonstrate encouraging findings in the assessment of ventricular recovery through the process we describe, we change their listing status to status 7 upon discussions to proceed with the explant process. Incorporating family goals and values is a critical component of these decisions. For some families, the uncertainty of recovery is challenging, and standard of care (listing for transplant) is preferred. As the field continues to develop a collective approach toward ventricular recovery, it will be important not to penalize those patients and families who choose to try for recovery before being actively listed for heart transplant. In the next iteration of the pediatric heart allocation system, consideration should be given to incorporating an incentive for attempting recovery into status assignments for patients on durable VAD support. Our experience also suggests a role for the use of concurrent procedures to promote explant in certain patients. Our cohort includes the use of cardiac resynchronization therapy at the time of explant in 2 infants with dilated cardiomyopathy and left bundle‐branch block that persisted through their ventricular recovery. Cardiac resynchronization therapy has an established place in the management of adults with heart failure, and although it is used less frequently in children, there is evidence that with thoughtful patient selection, it can provide substantial benefit for pediatric patients. , , , The incorporation of cardiac resynchronization therapy with VAD explant is novel and raises the possibility that the creative partnering of other procedures with explant could increase the population of explant candidates. Ton et al. report the use of mitral valve replacement in an adult with persistent mitral regurgitation to promote left VAD explant, and the Mitra Clip has been successfully used in a series of pediatric patients. , We posit that mitral valve interventions, both surgical and transcatheter, may be valuable for pediatric patients with persistent mitral regurgitation and evidence of systolic recovery. Limitations Our study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. This experience reflects the implementation of a process in a single center and includes a small population of patients who underwent VAD explant, which may limit the generalizability of our findings. Although there is a chance that some of the patients who underwent explant may have improved on medical therapy alone, the indications for VAD implantation at our center are aligned with national practice, leading us to believe that our experience is potentially generalizable. Furthermore, we do not have long‐term follow‐up on these patients, which precludes our ability to comment on the sustainability of ventricular recovery. Conclusions As the incidence of durable mechanical support in pediatric patients continues to grow, and the number of available heart transplant donors remains stable, it is imperative that we develop and implement a standardized approach to evaluation of ventricular recovery. Through a single‐center retrospective cohort study, we demonstrated that routinely scheduled testing, monitoring of laboratory values and growth parameters, use of GDMT, and interdisciplinary evaluation and discussion can help identify pediatric patients on VAD support who have had adequate ventricular recovery to undergo explant safely. This programmatic approach to promote and identify recovery yielded recovery in 26% of patients at our center on VAD. Whether the outcomes demonstrated in this small cohort are sustainable and can be replicated in a larger population is worthy of further investigation.
